parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Neutropenic sepsis
blurb: Suspect neutropenic sepsis early, give empiric antibiotics without delay and follow NICE CG151 from confirmation to discharge.
question: Mrs Collins, 57, arrives in the emergency department 10 days after chemotherapy for breast cancer. She feels shivery and unwell; her temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 108 and BP 104/70. Her full blood count result will take an hour. What should happen now?

teach.body: Neutropenia is a low neutrophil count, the white cells that fight bacterial infection; chemotherapy commonly causes it. NICE CG151 diagnoses neutropenic sepsis in people having anticancer treatment whose neutrophil count is 0.5 × 10^9/L or lower AND who have either a temperature higher than 38 °C or other signs or symptoms of clinically significant sepsis. Plain English: with almost no neutrophils, infection spreads fast and the usual signs (pus, redness, even fever) can be muted. So you treat on suspicion, not on proof.

teach.text: Do not wait for the neutrophil count, and do not wait for a fever. CG151: treat SUSPECTED neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and give empiric antibiotics immediately. Fever may be absent, and NG253 warns not to rely on temperature to rule sepsis in or out. (NG51 is withdrawn: adult sepsis guidance is NG253.)

teach.body: NICE NG253 says suspect neutropenic sepsis in anyone who becomes unwell and is having, or has had, systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days. It also applies to people receiving or who have received immunosuppressant treatment for reasons unrelated to cancer, using clinical judgement about whether past treatment could still cause neutropenia. Anticancer treatment includes chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Collins in the emergency department
teach.body: Mrs Collins, 57, is 10 days after chemotherapy. She is shivery, with temperature 37.4 °C, pulse 108 and BP 104/70. The triage nurse recognises suspected neutropenic sepsis despite the normal temperature. She escalates immediately, takes blood cultures (peripheral and from her PICC), FBC, kidney and liver function with albumin, CRP and lactate, and the prescribed piperacillin with tazobactam is given straight away, not after the FBC returns. The PICC stays in.

items: Suspect neutropenic sepsis in anyone unwell within 30 days of systemic anticancer treatment (or on immunosuppressants).
Treat suspected cases as an emergency: empiric antibiotics immediately, without waiting for the count.
Piperacillin with tazobactam monotherapy; no routine aminoglycoside or glycopeptide; keep the central line in.
Confirm: neutrophils 0.5 × 10^9/L or lower with temperature above 38 °C or other sepsis signs.
Risk-score within 24 h; switch to oral after 48 h if low risk; stop antibiotics when the sepsis has responded.

summary: You can now recognise suspected neutropenic sepsis early, act as an emergency without waiting for blood results, and apply NICE CG151 to antibiotics, investigations and central lines. You can also follow the risk-based plan from confirmation to switching and stopping antibiotics.

A.q: Mrs Okon, 66, has rheumatoid arthritis treated with an immunosuppressant. She has no history of cancer. She arrives feeling shivery and unwell. What does NICE NG253 advise about neutropenic sepsis?
options: Exclude it, as it applies to people with cancer
Consider it, using judgement about her immunosuppressant
Exclude it unless her temperature is above 38 °C
Consider it, if she has had radiotherapy in the last year
A.why: NG253 rec 1.1.10: suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell and are receiving or have received immunosuppressant treatment for reasons unrelated to cancer, using clinical judgement about whether the treatment may cause neutropenia.

whyNot.0: NG253 extends suspicion to immunosuppressant treatment unrelated to cancer.
whyNot.2: Fever is not required to suspect it; NICE warns not to rely on temperature.
whyNot.3: She has no cancer or radiotherapy; her immunosuppressant is the relevant factor.

A.q: Mr Hale is having chemotherapy. His neutrophil count is 0.4 × 10^9/L and his temperature is 37.6 °C, but he is confused with a BP of 86/50. Does he meet the NICE CG151 definition of neutropenic sepsis?
options: No, as his temperature is not above 38 °C
No, as his neutrophil count would need to be below 0.1
Yes, as his count is low and he has signs of sepsis
No, until a blood culture grows an organism
A.why: CG151 rec 1.4.4.1: neutrophils 0.5 × 10^9/L or lower with either a temperature above 38 °C or other signs or symptoms of clinically significant sepsis. Confusion and hypotension are such signs.

whyNot.0: A temperature above 38 °C is one route; other signs of significant sepsis also meet the definition.
whyNot.3: The diagnosis does not need a positive culture.

A.q: Ms Ward has a PICC line and is admitted with suspected neutropenic sepsis. A colleague suggests removing the PICC straight away as the likely source. What does NICE CG151 advise?
options: Remove it now and send the tip for culture
Remove it once the first dose of antibiotics has been given
Leave it in, as removal is not part of initial management
Replace it with a new central line at a different site
A.why: CG151 rec 1.4.3.4: do not remove central venous access devices as part of the initial empiric management of suspected neutropenic sepsis.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against removal as part of initial management.
whyNot.1: Timing the removal after the first dose is still removal during initial management.
whyNot.3: Replacing the line is also not part of initial empiric management.

B.q: Mr Sutton has suspected neutropenic sepsis and no allergies. His prescription is IV piperacillin with tazobactam plus IV gentamicin. There are no specific or local microbiological indications. What should the nurse do?
options: Query the gentamicin, as an aminoglycoside is not routinely added
Give both now, as dual therapy is the standard initial regimen here
Give the gentamicin first, as it acts more quickly
Delay both until the blood culture results are available tomorrow
B.why: CG151 recs 1.4.3.1–1.4.3.2: offer piperacillin with tazobactam monotherapy; do not offer an aminoglycoside as monotherapy or dual therapy for initial empiric treatment without specific indications.

whyNot.1: NICE recommends monotherapy, not dual therapy with an aminoglycoside.
whyNot.2: Gentamicin is not part of initial empiric therapy here.
whyNot.3: Antibiotics must be given immediately; cultures do not delay treatment.

B.q: Mr Lowe has suspected neutropenic sepsis but no cough, breathlessness or chest signs. A junior doctor asks for a chest X-ray before antibiotics are given. What does NICE CG151 advise?
options: Do the X-ray first so antibiotics can be targeted
Give antibiotics now; X-ray if clinically indicated
Do the X-ray and a CT chest before antibiotics
Wait for the X-ray report before taking any blood cultures
B.why: CG151 rec 1.4.1.1: give empiric antibiotics immediately; rec 1.4.2.2: do not perform a chest X-ray unless clinically indicated.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not delayed, and a routine X-ray is not recommended.
whyNot.2: Imaging does not delay treatment and is not routine.
whyNot.3: Blood cultures are part of the initial assessment and are not delayed for imaging.

B.q: Ms Ellis's neutropenic sepsis has responded to treatment: she is afebrile and well. Her neutrophil count is still 0.8 × 10^9/L. What does NICE CG151 say about her empiric antibiotics?
options: Continue them until her neutrophils exceed 1.0
Continue them for a fixed 14-day course
Switch them to long-term oral antibiotic prophylaxis at home
Stop them, as response matters more than the count
B.why: CG151 rec 1.5.4.2: discontinue empiric antibiotic therapy in patients whose neutropenic sepsis has responded to treatment, irrespective of neutrophil count.

whyNot.0: NICE says stop irrespective of the neutrophil count once the sepsis has responded.
whyNot.1: There is no fixed 14-day course in CG151.
whyNot.2: Long-term prophylaxis is not the CG151 plan after a responded episode.

C.q: Mrs Collins, 57, is in the emergency department 10 days after chemotherapy. She feels shivery and unwell; temperature 37.4 °C, pulse 108, BP 104/70. Blood cultures have been taken and her FBC will take an hour. Empiric antibiotics are prescribed. What should happen next?
options: Wait for the FBC to confirm she is neutropenic
Give paracetamol and recheck her temperature in an hour
Wait until her temperature rises above 38 °C
Give the antibiotics now without waiting for the FBC
C.why: CG151 rec 1.4.1.1: treat suspected neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and give empiric antibiotics immediately. Suspicion, not the count, triggers treatment.

whyNot.0: Waiting for the count delays treatment of a suspected emergency.
whyNot.1: Paracetamol can mask fever and does not treat sepsis; antibiotics are needed now.
whyNot.2: Fever may never appear; she already has signs of sepsis.

C.q: Mr Barnes has confirmed neutropenic sepsis and has had 48 hours of IV piperacillin with tazobactam. His observations are improving but the sepsis has not yet fully resolved, and an oncology specialist reassesses his risk of septic complications as low using a validated score. What does NICE CG151 recommend?
options: Continue IV antibiotics until his neutrophils recover
Stop antibiotics, as he is now at low risk
Switch from IV to oral antibiotics
Add a glycopeptide to cover his central line
C.why: CG151 rec 1.5.3.3: switch from IV to oral antibiotics after 48 hours in patients reassessed as low risk by a competent professional using a validated risk scoring system.

whyNot.0: Neutrophil recovery is not the trigger; low risk after 48 hours allows an oral switch.
whyNot.1: Low risk allows an oral switch; empiric antibiotics stop only once the sepsis has responded (rec 1.5.4.2), and his has not yet resolved.
whyNot.3: Empiric glycopeptides are not recommended without specific indications.

C.q: Mr Ahmed, 45, has acute leukaemia and is about to start chemotherapy that is expected to cause significant neutropenia. Which preventive measure does NICE CG151 recommend?
options: Routine G-CSF throughout every cycle of chemotherapy
Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis during the expected neutropenia
Piperacillin with tazobactam from day 1 of each cycle
Daily blood cultures throughout the period his neutrophil count is low
C.why: CG151 rec 1.2.1.1: for adults with acute leukaemias, stem cell transplants or solid tumours in whom significant neutropenia is anticipated, offer fluoroquinolone prophylaxis during the expected period of neutropenia.

whyNot.0: Rec 1.2.1.3: do not routinely offer G-CSF unless it is part of the regimen or to maintain dose intensity.
whyNot.2: Piperacillin with tazobactam is empiric treatment for suspected sepsis, not prophylaxis.
whyNot.3: Routine daily cultures are not a CG151 preventive measure.

reteach.title: Treat the suspicion, not the result
reteach.question: Why does a nurse give antibiotics before knowing the neutrophil count?

blocks.body: A person with very few neutrophils can go from 'a bit shivery' to septic shock within hours, often without a high temperature. That is why NICE says suspect neutropenic sepsis in anyone unwell within 30 days of systemic anticancer treatment, refer immediately, and give empiric antibiotics straight away. The count confirms the diagnosis later; it does not gate treatment.

blocks.text: Normal temperature does not rule it out. Unwell after chemotherapy = suspect neutropenic sepsis.

explain.body: Suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell and are having, or have had, systemic anticancer treatment in the last 30 days (or immunosuppressants). In the community, refer them immediately to secondary or tertiary care. Patients should know how to reach 24-hour specialist oncology advice.

test.q: Mr Dean feels unwell and shivery. His last chemotherapy was 3 weeks ago. Under NICE NG253, should neutropenic sepsis be suspected?
options: Yes, as anticancer treatment within 30 days counts
No, as neutropenia resolves within 14 days
No, unless his temperature rises to above 38 °C at home
Yes, once his full blood count result has come back
test.why: NG253 rec 1.1.10: suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell and have had systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days.

whyNot.1: NICE uses a 30-day window, not 14 days.
whyNot.2: Fever is not needed to suspect it.
whyNot.3: Suspicion is clinical; it does not wait for the count.

explain.body: Treat as an acute medical emergency and give empiric antibiotics immediately (piperacillin with tazobactam monotherapy). Initial assessment: history and examination; FBC, kidney and liver function including albumin, CRP, lactate and blood culture, with an extra peripheral culture if there is a central line.

test.q: Which set of blood tests does NICE CG151 include in the initial assessment of suspected neutropenic sepsis?
options: FBC, kidney and liver function, CRP, lactate, blood culture
FBC, clotting screen, troponin, blood glucose and blood gases
FBC, blood group and save, and thyroid function
FBC, amylase, ferritin, vitamin B12, folate and bone profile
test.why: CG151 rec 1.4.1.2: full blood count, kidney and liver function tests (including albumin), C-reactive protein, lactate and blood culture.

whyNot.1: Troponin and clotting are not the CG151 initial set.
whyNot.2: Group and save and thyroid function are not part of the CG151 set.
whyNot.3: Amylase, ferritin and B12 are not part of the CG151 set.

explain.body: Diagnose neutropenic sepsis when the neutrophil count is 0.5 × 10^9/L or lower AND there is either a temperature above 38 °C or other signs or symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis.

test.q: Which result confirms neutropenic sepsis in a person having chemotherapy, with no other sepsis signs?
options: Neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L, temperature 38.4 °C
Neutrophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, temperature 38.6 °C
Neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L, temperature 37.8 °C
Neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L, temperature 39.0 °C
test.why: Neutrophils 0.5 × 10^9/L or lower AND temperature above 38 °C: 0.4 and 38.4 °C meets both.

whyNot.1: A count of 0.9 is above the 0.5 threshold.
whyNot.2: 37.8 °C is not above 38 °C and there are no other sepsis signs.
whyNot.3: A count of 1.2 is above the 0.5 threshold.

explain.body: A professional competent in anticancer treatment complications assesses the risk of septic complications within 24 hours using a validated score (for example MASCC). Low risk: consider outpatient treatment. High risk: daily review and re-scoring; switch to oral after 48 hours if re-scored low. Do not switch antibiotics for unresponsive fever unless deteriorating or microbiology indicates.

test.q: Within what time of presentation does NICE CG151 say the risk of septic complications should be assessed with a validated scoring system?
options: Within 72 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 6 hours
Within 24 hours
test.why: CG151 rec 1.5.1.1: a competent professional should assess the risk of septic complications within 24 hours of presentation, using a validated risk scoring system.

whyNot.1: 48 hours is the point for considering an oral switch, not the first risk assessment.
whyNot.2: 6 hours is not the CG151 time frame; it is 24 hours.
